newsitem.title: USA: U.S. GDP growth rate seen slowing in 97--Rich. Fed.
newsitem.headline: U.S. GDP growth rate seen slowing in 97--Rich. Fed.

text.p: The U.S. economy is expanding rapidly, but Gross Domestic Product growth is likely to slow down to slightly below 3.0 by year end, said the head of the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond Alfred Broaddus.
"The economy is growing rapidly," Broaddus told an audience here at the Southern State Treasurers conference.
Citing a consensus of professional forecasters, Broaddus added, however, "GDP growth rate is expected to slow a little bit ... coming a little under 3.0 percent in 1997."
Broaddus said the consensus forecast suggest U.S. labor markets will remain tight, with the unemployment rate dropping slightly to around 5.0 percent by late 1997.
"Job markets are expected to remain tight, the unemployment rate is expected ... to end the year somewhere around 5.0 percent," Broaddus said.

"Well, the forecast is for a modest increase in the core rate of inflation this year, but really only a modest, marginal increase, with the core CPI remaining below 3.0 percent at an annual rate in 1997," he added.
The Richmond Fed chief said the current scenario suggests the risks remain tilted to the upside for the U.S. economy.

"There are some downside risks, but ladies and gentleman, as I look at all of the factors as best as I can I would have to say I think the risk ... is more heavily weighted to the upside, specially with respect with prospects of prices and inflation," Broaddus said.
The Richmond Fed president also said that if demand remains strong, job insecurity -- which has been seen by many as one of the key factors holding wage inflation down -- is likely to fade.
"If the household and business demand remain strong, as strong as it has been, and labor markets remain as tight as they have been ... sooner or later that job insecurity is going to fade," he said.

Broaddus said the central bank's goal of achieving price stability will reinforce economic growth in the long term. "The best anti-inflationary policy is a profoundly pro-growth policy rather than the other way around," he said.
"We are fighting inflation to try to provide the necessary monetary foundation for strong, and, hopefully, stronger growth in the economy," He said.
Broaddus reiterated that the Federal Reserve monetary policy must remain pre-emptive and stay "ahead of the inflation curve."
The Richmond Fed president praised a decision by Britain's newly-elected Labour government to hand responsibility for setting interest rates to the Bank of England (BOE).

"To the extent that the British have now moved to getting the Bank of England ... more independence than it has had; that raises the prospects that the British will be able to maintain the very substantial progress they've made in recent years in bringing their inflation rate to much lower levels," he said.
